title: Why More Practice Tests Did Not Produce More Learning
passage:
A tutoring center preparing students for entrance examinations believed strongly in practice tests. Students completed a full mock exam every Saturday, received a score, and compared their ranking with previous weeks. The system created a sense of seriousness, and families appreciated seeing numerical progress. Yet teachers noticed a troubling pattern. Some students took many tests without improving on the types of questions they repeatedly missed.

The center reviewed how students used feedback. After each test, answers were returned with correct choices and brief explanations. Many students checked the score first, looked at the ranking, and then put the paper away. A few corrected mistakes carefully, but there was no structured time for doing so. The center had created repeated measurement without ensuring repeated learning.

Teachers divided students into two trial groups. Both completed the same number of questions over a month. One group continued taking a full mock exam each week. The other took two full exams during the month and used the remaining Saturdays for targeted review. During review sessions, students classified errors: knowledge missing, question misread, calculation mistake, poor time management, or uncertain strategy. They then solved new questions addressing the same weakness.

At first, some students in the review group disliked the change because they had fewer fresh scores. Without a weekly number, they felt less certain about progress. Teachers explained that a score is a sample of performance, not the performance itself. A student can become better at one weak skill even if a later test happens to contain harder material and the total score barely changes.

The error categories were also imperfect. A wrong answer could have several causes. A student might not know a formula and also rush because time was short. Teachers told students to choose the cause that would be most useful for deciding what to do next. The classification was a planning tool, not a scientific diagnosis.

After eight weeks, the targeted-review group showed stronger improvement on repeated skill areas, although overall mock scores varied from week to week. They also became faster at explaining why they had missed a question. The weekly-test group gained familiarity with exam conditions and improved time management, but some students continued making the same conceptual errors. Neither approach was useless; they trained different things.

The center changed its program. Full mock exams remained important for practicing pacing, endurance, and decision-making under realistic conditions. However, they were scheduled less frequently and followed by a mandatory correction cycle. Students had to redo missed questions without looking at the answer, explain the cause of each error, and solve at least one new problem requiring the same idea. Teachers checked whether the second attempt showed real understanding rather than memorization.

Rankings were also redesigned. They were still available because entrance examinations are competitive, but the main student dashboard emphasized accuracy by skill, recurring error types, and whether previously weak areas had improved. This reduced some obsession with small week-to-week rank changes. A student moving from 42nd to 38th place might feel successful even if the difference reflected other students' performance rather than meaningful learning.

Families initially asked why there were fewer full scores to compare. The center shared examples showing how targeted review connected mistakes to later success. Over time, many parents accepted that less frequent testing did not mean less serious preparation.

The experience clarified the difference between assessment and instruction. A practice test is valuable because it reveals performance under certain conditions. But taking another test immediately does not automatically repair what the first one revealed. Measurement can guide learning, yet only if there is a process between measurements that changes knowledge or strategy.

The center eventually used a simple phrase with students: ‘Test, learn, retest.’ The middle word mattered most. Without it, repeated testing could become an activity that generated increasingly familiar score reports while leaving the underlying weaknesses almost untouched. With it, a lower score could become useful evidence rather than a judgment, and a mistake could become the starting point for a specific next step.
translation:
入試対策塾では毎週土曜に模擬試験を行い、点数と順位で進歩を確認していました。しかし教師は、何度受けても同じ種類の問題を間違える生徒がいることに気づきました。

答案には正答と短い解説が付いていましたが、多くの生徒はまず点数と順位を見て、そのまま片付けていました。テストという『測定』は繰り返していても、学習の修正過程が保証されていなかったのです。

そこで一か月の総問題数は同じにし、一方は毎週模試、もう一方は模試を二回に減らして残りを弱点復習に使いました。復習では、知識不足、読み違い、計算ミス、時間配分、解法判断などに誤りを分類し、同じ弱点を使う新しい問題を解きました。

復習組の一部は毎週新しい点数が出ないことを不安に感じました。教師は、点数は能力そのものではなく、その時の問題を使った標本だと説明しました。弱点が改善していても、次の模試が難しければ総点は変わらないことがあります。

誤り分類も完全ではありません。一問に知識不足と焦りが同時に関わることもあります。そこで『最も役立つ次の行動を決める原因』を選ぶ計画道具として使いました。

八週間後、弱点復習組は繰り返し出る技能で改善が大きく、なぜ間違えたか説明する力も上がりました。毎週模試組は本番形式や時間配分に慣れましたが、概念的な同じ誤りを続ける生徒もいました。両方に価値があり、鍛えるものが違ったのです。

塾は模試を残しつつ頻度を少し減らし、必ず『訂正サイクル』を付けました。答えを見ずに解き直す、原因を説明する、同じ考えを使う新問を解く、という流れです。単なる正答暗記ではなく理解を確認しました。

順位は残しましたが、画面の中心を技能別正答率、繰り返す誤り、弱点改善へ移しました。順位変動は他人の結果にも左右されるためです。

保護者にも、模試が減ることは準備が弱くなることではなく、測定結果を学習へ変える時間を増やすことだと説明しました。

この経験は評価と指導の違いを示します。テストは現在の状態を明らかにしますが、次のテストを受けるだけでは弱点は直りません。測定と測定の間に知識や戦略を変える過程が必要です。

塾は『テストする、学ぶ、再テストする』という言葉を使うようになりました。最も重要なのは真ん中の『学ぶ』です。それがあれば低い点数も判決ではなく、次の具体的行動を教える証拠になります。
